identity.title: Addressing Misspecification in Simulation-based Inference through Data-driven Calibration

problem.claim: Make simulation-based inference reliable when the available simulator is misspecified.

gap.claim: Misspecification can harm SBI reliability, while existing approaches do not provide a stated way to learn the misspecification without additional assumptions on its nature.

contributions.claim: Introduces robust posterior estimation (RoPE), using a small real-world calibration set of ground-truth parameter measurements.
Formulates the misspecification gap as an optimal-transport problem between learned representations of real and simulated observations.

stated_novelty.claim: RoPE learns a model of misspecification without placing additional assumptions on its nature.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that combining the calibration set with optimal transport provides a controllable balance between calibrated uncertainty and informative inference, even with severely misspecified simulators.

Across four synthetic tasks and two real-world problems with ground-truth labels, the authors report that RoPE outperforms baselines and consistently produces informative, calibrated credible intervals.

narrative_sequence.summary: SBI is presented as a workhorse for inferring parameters of stochastic simulators.
Simulator misspecification is identified as a reliability barrier to SBI adoption.
RoPE uses real-world calibration measurements and optimal transport between learned real and simulated representations to model misspecification.
The calibration set and optimal transport are reported to balance uncertainty calibration with informative inference under severe misspecification.
Reported tests cover four synthetic tasks and two labeled real-world problems, with comparisons against baselines.

source_observation.claim: The abstract connects a controllable inference trade-off to two explicit ingredients: a real-world calibration set and optimal transport.

lessons.interpretation: Naming which components control a desired trade-off can make a method claim more mechanistically interpretable.
lessons.application: When proposing a robustness method, state which data or algorithmic components govern each target property and how they are intended to interact.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the abstract cannot support a component-to-property link or when the interaction is purely conjectural.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify calibration-set size, baseline identities, quantitative gains, or how the controllable balance is tuned.
The reported real-world tasks, misspecification severity, and credible-interval evaluation details are unspecified.
